evidence.title: Qurta I–III (Upper Egypt): North Africa's oldest dated Pleistocene rock art
evidence.dateBasis: OSL dating of aeolian silt sealing deeply patinated naturalistic sandstone panels (Huyge et al. 2011).
evidence.summary: Over 180 deeply pecked and hammered Upper Paleolithic panels along the Nile valley above Kom Ombo depict heroic wild cattle (aurochs), hippopotami and wetland birds in natural profile.
evidence.limits: Minimum age >15 ka from overlying Nile–aeolian sediments; actual carving may date back toward ~17–19 ka.

evidence.title: Wadi Sura II — Cave of Beasts (Gilf Kebir, SW Egypt): Humid-Sahara hand stencils & floating figures
evidence.dateBasis: Association with mid-Holocene humid-phase playas and excavated hearth radiocarbon dates at the Gilf Kebir foothills.
evidence.summary: Over 5,000 red, yellow and white mineral-pigment paintings pack a deep sandstone alcove with negative hand stencils, archers and enigmatic 'headless beast' beings.
evidence.limits: No direct pigment binder radiocarbon dates exist yet; dates follow regional African Humid Period geomorphology.

evidence.title: Wadi Mathendous & In Galgien (Fezzan, Libya): Monumental Bubalus & Nile crocodile engravings
evidence.dateBasis: Pleistocene-to-Early Holocene Bubalus-style patina, savanna megafauna ecology and Messak Settafet archaeology.
evidence.summary: Sweeping sandstone cliff meanders cut by fossil Sahara rivers preserve monumental deep-grooved elephants, rhinoceros, hippopotami, giant extinct buffalo (Pelorovis) and crocodiles.
evidence.limits: Varnish sequences establish relative horizons; exact century boundaries between wild-fauna and pastoral phases remain debated.

evidence.title: Dabous Giraffes (Aïr Mountains, Niger): World's largest monumental animal petroglyphs
evidence.dateBasis: Early Pastoral–Kiffian/Tenerian humid Sahara chronological window anchored to Ténéré lake stands.
evidence.summary: Two life-sized low-relief giraffes over 5 meters tall—leashed with delicate lines to tiny human figures—gleam across an inclined sandstone outcrop in Niger's Ténéré margin.
evidence.limits: Stylistic attribution to humid-phase Saharan herders; surface sandstone exposes images to wind abrasion.

evidence.title: Tiout & Ain Sefra (Saharan Atlas, Algeria): Neolithic rams & elephant friezes
evidence.dateBasis: Correlation with Capsian–Neolithic humid Maghreb steppe art and Saharan Atlas Bubalus-period typology.
evidence.summary: High Atlas sandstone slabs overlook the Ksour steppe with deeply carved hunters, wild elephants, lions, and collared sacred rams with solar spheroid headdresses.
evidence.limits: Pre-dates Libyco-Berber script horizons; exact overlap between late Capsian and early herding groups remains studied.

evidence.title: Oukaïmeden & Yagour Plateau (High Atlas, Morocco): High-altitude Bronze halberds & shields
evidence.dateBasis: Diagnostic Iberian–North African Bronze Age halberd, dagger, disk-shield and Libyco-Berber motif typology at 2,600 m pastures.
evidence.summary: Summer-pasture red sandstone meadows in the High Atlas hold over 2,000 Bronze-to-Iron Age engravings of metallic halberds, daggers, circular shields, cattle and sun glyphs.
evidence.limits: Seasonal snowpack and weathering limit organic residues; typology anchors metalwork images to Atlantic Bronze Age networks.

evidence.title: Maloti-Drakensberg — Game Pass & Kamberg Shelters (South Africa): San polychrome trance murals
evidence.dateBasis: Accelerator Mass Spectrometry dates on carbon black/oxalate crusts and UNESCO WHC #985 ethnography with /Xam & Maloti San descendants.
evidence.summary: High Cave Sandstone overhangs hold more than 35,000 San finely shaded polychrome eland, hunters and transformative rainmaking dances central to /Xam San spirituality.
evidence.limits: Surviving surface paintings skew toward the past 3,000 years due to natural exfoliation of damp sandstone overhangs.

evidence.title: Cederberg — Stadsaal & Sevilla Shelters (Western Cape, South Africa): Finger-dots, eland & elephants
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified LSA shelter sequences and stylistic seriation across fine-brush San paintings and later Khoekhoen finger-dots.
evidence.summary: Wind-sculpted Table Mountain sandstone arches shelter red-ochre fine-line eland processions, elephants, hooked-head human groups and hundreds of positive handprints.
evidence.limits: Pre-contact panels predate well-known 18th-century colonial resistance art elsewhere in the Cederberg.

evidence.title: Wildebeest Kuil & Karoo /Xam Engravings (Northern Cape, South Africa): Dolerite boulder art
evidence.dateBasis: Dolerite/andesite patina contrast, /Xam Bleek–Lloyd ethnography, and Later Stone Age Wilton assemblages at Springbok/Klipfontein outcrops.
evidence.summary: Iron-rich dolerite boulders rising across the arid Karoo plateau carry thousands of delicately pecked and scraped rhinos, eland, dancing shamans and rain creatures.
evidence.limits: Varnish repatination shows wide multi-millennial span; fine scratched images are younger than deepest-pecked outlines.

evidence.title: Chongoni Rock-Art Area (Dedza, Malawi): UNESCO #476 BaTwa geometrics & Chewa Nyau murals
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #476 archaeological survey separating red BaTwa hunter-forager geometrics from superimposed Iron Age Chewa white-clay Nyau masquerade motifs.
evidence.summary: 127 granite shelter walls amid forested inselbergs preserve Central Africa's densest gallery: early red-ochre concentric webs painted by BaTwa foragers beneath dramatic white-clay Chewa women's initiation and Nyau secret-society murals.
evidence.limits: Earlier BaTwa paintings remain indirectly dated; living Chewa oral knowledge interprets white-clay imagery.

evidence.title: Nyero Rock Shelters (Kumi, Eastern Uganda): Red-ochre concentric circles & canoe overhangs
evidence.dateBasis: Pan-East African Later Stone Age geometric rock-art horizon (red concentric rings, acacia pods, crescentic canoes) beneath granite overhangs.
evidence.summary: Deep granite overhangs facing Lake Kyoga wetlands display vivid crimson concentric wheels, comb shapes and high-prowed dugouts attributed to ancestral Twa/hunter-fisher communities.
evidence.limits: Uncertain direct age; overlaps broader Lake Victoria red geometric rock-art horizon spanning terminal LSA to Iron Age.

evidence.title: Mwela Rocks (Kasama, Northern Zambia): Over 1,000 quartzite ridge paintings
evidence.dateBasis: Wilton–Nachikufan Later Stone Age deposits and stylistic superposition across >700 northern Zambian shelters.
evidence.summary: Quartzite kopjes above Chambeshi wetlands shelter over a thousand red and white schematic sun-circles, grid nets and rare naturalistic antelopes.
evidence.limits: Nachikufan lithic associations date back millennia, while white schematic panels overlap Later Iron Age traditions.

evidence.title: Spitzkoppe ('Bushman's Paradise') & Erongo (Namibia): Granite inselberg overhangs
evidence.dateBasis: Wilton-age Namib margin charcoal hearths and stylistic parallel with nearby Brandberg/Dâures and Twyfelfontein sequences.
evidence.summary: Soaring granite domes emerging from the Namib plains shelter richly painted yellow, white and red giraffes, zebras, rhinos and ceremonial lines hidden inside cool ceiling overhangs.
evidence.limits: Exfoliation and modern desert dust leave most surviving murals within the last ~4,000 years.

evidence.title: Dhambalin & Dhagah Khure (Somaliland): Earliest horned cattle & giraffe shelter panels
evidence.dateBasis: Ethiopian-Arabian humpless cattle typology paired with wild giraffes (rare in Horn rock art) before camel introduction (Mire 2008).
evidence.summary: Sandstone rock shelters across Somaliland preserve vibrant red, white and black humpless longhorn cattle, archers, dogs, antelopes and the Horn of Africa's earliest known painted giraffes.
evidence.limits: Chronology rests on faunal succession (pre-zebu cattle and wild savanna fauna) rather than direct pigment radiocarbon dates.

evidence.title: Laga Oda & Porc-Epic Shelters (Hararghe, Ethiopia): Highland pastoral cattle paintings
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated Later Stone Age & early domestic-cattle faunal sequence paired with Ethiopian-Arabian schematic stylized cattle cliff murals.
evidence.summary: Limestone cliff galleries near Dire Dawa display hundreds of abstract, fork-legged and humpless cattle symbols above stratified highland LSA–Neolithic occupation debris.
evidence.limits: Exact paint age remains indirectly linked to nearby domestic-bovine bone radiocarbon horizons.

evidence.title: Birnin Kudu & Geji (Jigawa–Bauchi, Nigeria): West African humpless cattle & rock gongs
evidence.dateBasis: Pastoral West African humpless cattle depictions and ring-tuned granite acoustic 'rock gongs' linked to Nok-era northern savanna sites.
evidence.summary: Granite kopje overhangs at Birnin Kudu and Geji show West Africa's finest surviving humpless short-horned cattle paintings alongside natural granite boulders hammered as ceremonial rock gongs.
evidence.limits: Mineral-iron pigments lack organic binders for direct AMS dating; age derives from cattle breed morphology and Early Iron pottery.

evidence.title: Bidzar Marble Outcrops (Northern Cameroon): Engraved geometric cosmograms
evidence.dateBasis: Contextual correlation with Late Neolithic / Early Iron Age Chad Basin stone-and-iron settlement horizons.
evidence.summary: Low-lying bands of pale crystalline marble in northern Cameroon bear hundreds of deeply pecked geometric rings, spokes and rayed sunbursts across open outcrops.
evidence.limits: Age rests on regional settlement correlations around the Benue–Mayo Louti watershed.

evidence.title: Epona & Elarmekora / Lopé-Okanda (Gabon): Equatorial rainforest corridor petroglyphs
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1147 savanna-forest corridor ironworking hearth dates directly flanking over 1,800 geometric iron-chiseled carvings.
evidence.summary: Ice-age savanna refugia islands embedded inside Gabon's equatorial forest preserve >1,800 spirals, blades, throwing knives and lizard motifs pecked by early Bantu-speaking ironworkers along the Ogooué River.
evidence.limits: Metal toolmarks tie main engraving surge to Early Iron Age expansion along the Ogooué migration artery.

evidence.title: The Camel Site (Al-Jawf, Saudi Arabia): Monumental ~5600–5200 BCE Neolithic camel reliefs
evidence.dateBasis: Portable OSL dating of fallen blocks, limestone patina, weathering indices and lithic tool-mark matches (Guagnin et al. 2021 JAS: Reports).
evidence.summary: More than twenty monumental, life-sized three-dimensional high reliefs of wild dromedaries and equids carved onto towering sandstone spurs during North Arabia's Humid Holocene.
evidence.limits: Severe erosion truncated lower legs; OSL dates place initial sculpting unexpectedly deep in the sixth millennium BCE.

evidence.title: Kilwa & Wisad Pools (Badia Black Desert, Jordan–Saudi): Basalt kites, oryx & Safaitic panels
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified Late Neolithic basalt architecture, desert-kite trap surveys, and thousands of dated Safaitic desert inscriptions beside wildlife drawings.
evidence.summary: Desert basalt fields spanning eastern Jordan into northern Saudi Arabia turn boulders into visual diaries—Neolithic hunters, ibex, desert-kite game traps, lions and bilingual Safaitic verses.
evidence.limits: Multi-millennial accumulation from Late Neolithic hunters through Iron Age and Safaitic nomads.

evidence.title: Wadi Rum Canyons (Jordan): UNESCO #1377 Thamudic & Nabataean sandstone galleries
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1377 association uniting Bronze Age hunting friezes with over 25,000 petroglyphs and 20,000 Thamudic/Nabataean caravan inscriptions.
evidence.summary: Soaring red sandstone canyon walls at Khazʿali and Anfeeshieh document five millennia of ibex chases, domesticated camel caravans, footsteps and South Semitic desert inscriptions.
evidence.limits: Continuity extends past 100 BCE into late Nabataean and early Islamic periods.

evidence.title: Har Karkom & Timna Valley (Negev–Arava): Limestone sanctuary & copper-miner rock panels
evidence.dateBasis: Bronze Age desert-shrine pavements and Egyptian-Midianite Timna smelting camp stratigraphy flanking engraved chariot and ibex cliffs.
evidence.summary: Black-varnished limestone outcrops on the Negev highlands and Timna copper canyons combine Chalcolithic/Bronze prayer circles, ibex hunts, and Late Bronze battle chariots.
evidence.limits: Patinated desert varnish styles overlap widely across Sinai–Negev nomadic cycles.

evidence.title: Ḥimā Cultural Area (Najran, Saudi Arabia): UNESCO #1619 7,000-year hunting & script cliffs
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1619 documented rock-art and epigraphic inventory across >550 sandstone cliffs on the incense-route oasis rim.
evidence.summary: One of the world's largest desert rock-art archives stretches along ancient camel wells: long-horned Neolithic cattle, ostriches, spears and dancers right beside Musnad and Thamudic inscriptions.
evidence.limits: Later scripts overlay deeper Neolithic patinations well into the Common Era.

evidence.title: Jebel Jassassiyeh (Northern Qatar): Coastal limestone boats, ostriches & cupules
evidence.dateBasis: Comparison with Bronze/Iron Age Dilmun coastal surveys and game-board/dhow motif horizons along the Arabian Gulf.
evidence.summary: Weather-worn coastal limestone ridges above the Gulf shore hold nearly 900 carvings—double rows of game-board cupules, rosettes, sea turtles, desert ostriches and overhead-view sailing craft.
evidence.limits: Boat typologies span both ancient Gulf craft and later pearling dhows; exact carving dates remain debated.

evidence.title: Öküzini & Beldibi Caves (Antalya, Anatolia): Late Glacial engraved walls & cobbles
evidence.dateBasis: AMS radiocarbon stratigraphy of Epipaleolithic layers containing engraved river cobbles and adjacent karst cave-wall schematics.
evidence.summary: Mediterranean coastal caves near Antalya preserve Anatolia's earliest post-Ice Age visual records: schematic bulls and geometric combs pecked onto cave walls alongside finely incised antler/cobble hunting scenes.
evidence.limits: Cave-wall humidity erased fragile pigments; incised cobbles provide tight stratigraphic anchor ages.

evidence.title: Teymareh Rock Art Valleys (Khomeyn, Central Iran): 20,000+ Zagros ibex & hunting cliffs
evidence.dateBasis: Comparative stylistic and archaic inscription seriation across ~20,000+ sandstone petroglyphs bordering the central Zagros foothills.
evidence.summary: Dense sandstone canyon trails in Markazi Province preserve tens of thousands of soaring-horned Iranian ibex, leopards, horseback riders and early Elamite-to-Parthian engravings.
evidence.limits: Lack of direct varnish calibration makes oldest Pleistocene/Early Holocene claims contested; core corpus anchors in Chalcolithic–Iron horizons.

evidence.title: Gobustan Rock Art Cultural Landscape (Azerbaijan): UNESCO #1076 reed boats & Pleistocene-to-Iron cliffs
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1076 correlation between raised Caspian terrace shorelines, excavated Epipaleolithic flint levels and 6,000+ limestone block engravings.
evidence.summary: Semi-arid Caspian boulder terraces above ancient higher shorelines showcase massive aurochs, wild goats, ceremonial line dancers ('Yalli') and multi-oared solar-prowed reed boats.
evidence.limits: Multi-period boulder collapses span terminal Paleolithic hunters down through Bronze Age herdsmen and Roman legion inscriptions.

evidence.title: Ain Mallaha / Eynan (Upper Jordan Valley): Natufian year-round hamlet & lime-lined houses
evidence.dateBasis: Extensive C14 charcoal/bone chronology spanning Early, Late and Final Natufian semi-subterranean limestone houses beside Lake Hula.
evidence.summary: Before full cereal domestication, Natufian communities built permanent stone-walled circular huts, hearths, plastered storage silos and dog burials along fish-and-gazelle-rich wetlands.
evidence.limits: Illustrates sedentism preceding agriculture across the Levant.

evidence.title: Tell Abu Hureyra (Middle Euphrates, Syria): Epipaleolithic wild-rye cultivators to 6,000-person Neolithic town
evidence.dateBasis: AMS radiocarbon series on charred grains and multi-meter tell stratigraphy documenting Younger Dryas drought response and intensive cultivation.
evidence.summary: Starting as an Epipaleolithic pit-dwelling village harvesting >150 wild seeds, Abu Hureyra evolved into one of the world's largest Pre-Pottery Neolithic mudbrick farming towns covering ~12 hectares.
evidence.limits: Excavated prior to Tabqa Dam flooding; debate continues over whether early Younger Dryas rye grains reflect full domestication or wild tending.

evidence.title: Jerf el-Ahmar & Mureybet (Middle Euphrates, Syria): PPNA communal buildings & incised stone plaques
evidence.dateBasis: PPNA radiocarbon sequence tying round-to-rectangular domestic architecture with monumental sunken community granary-sanctuaries and pictographic stones.
evidence.summary: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A villagers excavated huge communal stone-and-mudbrick subterranean structures alongside small incised limestone plaques bearing snake, vulture and arrow pictograms.
evidence.limits: Community coordination predates urban states by 5,000 years.

evidence.title: Çayönü Tepesi & Nevalı Çori (Upper Tigris–Euphrates, Anatolia): Terrazzo ritual floors & early metallurgy
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon sequence spanning Round, Grill-Plan, Channeled, Skull-Building and Cell-Plan phases with cold-hammered native copper.
evidence.summary: Upper Mesopotamian Neolithic settlements innovated monumental T-pillar shrines, stained lime-terrazzo floors, pig domestication and some of humanity's earliest native-copper beads and awls.
evidence.limits: Chronology across building sub-phases derives from >50 C14 dates.

evidence.title: ʿAin Ghazal (Amman, Jordan): PPNB ~15-hectare mega-village & lime-plaster human statues
evidence.dateBasis: Deep PPNB-to-Yarmoukian radiocarbon chronology anchoring two famous ceremonial pits holding 30 monumental reed-core lime-plaster human statues (Rollefson; Grissom 2000).
evidence.summary: Two-headed and wide-eyed lime-plaster human statues up to 1 meter tall were buried beneath house floors in one of the Levant's largest Neolithic towns (~3,000 inhabitants at peak).
evidence.limits: Demonstrates specialized plaster technology and ancestral imagery over a millennium before pottery towns scaled up.

evidence.title: Beidha & Basta (Southern Jordan Highlands): Multi-room terraced PPNB farming towns
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon dates from corridor-basement craft workshops at Beidha (near Petra) and towering stone wall rooms at Basta.
evidence.summary: Villagers built semi-subterranean workshops and remarkably well-preserved multi-room masonry houses supported on stone channel subfloors across arid southern Jordanian sandstone valleys.
evidence.limits: Late PPNB demographic growth was followed by localized highland reorganization.

evidence.title: Qalʿat Jarmo (Chamchamal, Iraqi Kurdistan): Upland Zagros Neolithic farming village
evidence.dateBasis: Robert Braidwood's landmark multi-disciplinary C14 & botanical project establishing early upland village agriculture across 16 occupational levels.
evidence.summary: About 25 mudbrick tauf houses housed ~150 villagers cultivating emmer, einkorn and lentils alongside domesticated goats and early painted ceramics high in the Zagros foothills.
evidence.limits: Early C14 runs had wide error bars; subsequent Zagros studies refine the ~7500–6000 BCE horizon.

evidence.title: Ali Kosh (Deh Luran Plain, SW Iran): Early lowland Zagros irrigation transition village
evidence.dateBasis: Bus Mordeh, Ali Kosh and Mohammad Jaffar phase chronology linking transhumant goat herding to nascent lowland floodwater cereal cultivation.
evidence.summary: Mudbrick huts overlooking Khuzestan marshes track how winter herders stabilized year-round cereal harvests using marsh-edge moisture and Anatolian obsidian trade.
evidence.limits: Later alluvial deposition covers many sister lowland Deh Luran hamlets.

evidence.title: Susa & Chogha Mish (Susiana Plain, SW Iran): 6,000-year Elamite–Achaemenid city sequence
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1455 continuous tell stratigraphy spanning Susiana Neolithic painted goblets, Proto-Elamite tablets, Middle Elamite ziggurats and Achaemenid–Seleucid Susa.
evidence.summary: Rising beside the Karkheh and Dez rivers, Chogha Mish and Susa trace six uninterrupted millennia from archaic Susiana mudbrick farms to the Elamite world capital and Persian winter palace.
evidence.limits: Occupation extends onward through Parthian and Sasanian centuries.

evidence.title: Tell Arpachiyah & Hassuna–Halaf Villages (Upper Tigris, Iraq): Stone-founded tholoi & kiln craft
evidence.dateBasis: Stratigraphic Ceramic Neolithic sequence defining Northern Mesopotamian Hassuna, Samarra and polychrome Halaf luxury craft workshops.
evidence.summary: Circular cobbled-foundation tholoi topped by mudbrick vaults produced breathtaking polychrome pottery plates, carved steatite amulets and administrative stamp seals centuries before cities.
evidence.limits: Burned 'Pottery House' TT6 remains a benchmark for late Halaf exchange.

evidence.title: Nippur & Kish (Central Mesopotamia, Iraq): Sumerian religious capital & earliest dynastic tablets
evidence.dateBasis: Continuous Ubaid-through-Parthian stratigraphy preserving the Ekur Temple of Enlil and tens of thousands of Sumerian literary and administrative tablets.
evidence.summary: Though never seat of a single territorial empire, Nippur served Sumer and Akkad for millennia as Mesopotamia's supreme cult sanctuary where kings sought legitimacy and scribes copied epic poetry.
evidence.limits: Continued active beyond 100 BCE into Parthian and Sasanian eras.

evidence.title: Mari / Tell Hariri (Middle Euphrates, Syria): Circular river-canal metropolis & Palace murals
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated circular dike city (~1.9 km diameter), 25,000+ cuneiform letters, and painted wall frescoes inside the Grand Royal Palace burned by Hammurabi.
evidence.summary: Engineered along a navigation canal paralleling the Euphrates, Mari connected Persian Gulf tin and Arabian horses with Levantine cedar—and preserved rare Bronze Age palatial wall paintings.
evidence.limits: Sacked and burned c. 1759 BCE; later Seleucid–Parthian levels remain sparse.

evidence.title: Ebla / Tell Mardikh (Northern Syria): Early Bronze Kingdom & 17,000-tablet Royal Archive
evidence.dateBasis: Direct epigraphic archive in Palace G (c. 2400–2300 BCE) writing both Sumerian and the oldest documented West Semitic (Eblaite) state administration.
evidence.summary: Sixteen-meter earthen ramparts and Royal Palace G show a booming inland Syrian kingdom brokering textiles, olive oil, lapis lazuli and silver between Egypt, Mari and Anatolia.
evidence.limits: Major city destroyed c. 1600 BCE.

evidence.title: Megiddo & Hazor (Jezreel & Galilee, Levant): UNESCO #1108 Bronze-to-Iron Age fortified tels
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1108 thirty-layer tell mounds spanning Canaanite temples, chariot gates, deep bedrock water tunnels and Assyrian provincial quarters.
evidence.summary: Guarding the Carmel mountain pass between Egypt and Damascus, Megiddo and Hazor preserve monumental ashlar six-chambered gates and subterranean rock-cut spring shafts.
evidence.limits: Multi-period chronology debates around 10th vs 9th century BCE Iron IIA strata continue.

evidence.title: Alaca Höyük & Kültepe-Kanesh (Central Anatolia): Royal tombs & Karum merchant tablets
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO-listed Kültepe archive of >23,000 Old Assyrian clay contracts (c. 1950–1700 BCE) paired with Alaca Höyük Early Bronze electrum-and-bronze sun standards.
evidence.summary: From Hatti royal shaft graves holding cast bronze stags and solar discs to Karum Kanesh's bilingual Assyrian merchant colony, Central Anatolia pioneered international credit networks.
evidence.limits: Hittite Empire transition ended the Karum network c. 1700 BCE while Alaca continued as a major Hittite gate city.

evidence.title: Tushpa / Van Citadel & Altıntepe (Eastern Anatolia): Urartian stone aqueducts & bronze works
evidence.dateBasis: Urartian cuneiform foundation stelae of Sarduri I, Menua's 51-km Shamram Canal still watering Van, and rock-cut royal cliff tombs.
evidence.summary: Carved out of a dramatic limestone ridge above Lake Van, Tushpa anchored the alpine Kingdom of Urartu with fortified terraced reservoirs, iron weapons and fine bronze shields.
evidence.limits: Succeeding Achaemenid satrapy continued on the plain before Hellenistic transition.

evidence.title: Qalʿat al-Bahrain — Ancient Harbour & Capital of Dilmun (UNESCO #1192)
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1192 stratified 12-meter tell spanning Dilmun City I–III, Kassite, Neo-Assyrian and Tylos Hellenistic harbor fortresses.
evidence.summary: Freshwater submarine springs made Dilmun the sacred paradise and commercial entrepôt bridging Mesopotamian grain/textiles, Omani Magan copper and Indus carnelian.
evidence.limits: Harbor remained active well after 100 BCE through Tylos and Islamic centuries.

evidence.title: Bat, Al-Khutm & Hili Oasis (Oman/UAE): UNESCO #434 Umm an-Nar towers & copper hubs
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #434 Hafit & Umm an-Nar stone watchtowers, collective ashlar tombs and Early Bronze falaj irrigation–copper workshops of ancient Magan.
evidence.summary: At the foot of the Hajar Mountains, monumental circular stone towers built around deep wells coordinated copper smelting destined for Sumerian ships at Dilmun.
evidence.limits: Oasis settlements persisted into Wadi Suq and Iron Age falaj transformations.

evidence.title: Shabwa & Timnaʿ (Hadhramaut & Qataban, Yemen): Fortified South Arabian incense capitals
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated mudbrick–stone-frame multi-story urban palaces, salt-mine networks and Sabaean–Qatabanian–Hadhrami monumental inscriptions.
evidence.summary: Sitting at the desert gate of Wadi Hadhramaut, Shabwa and Qataban's Timnaʿ channeled frankincense and myrrh northward along camel routes toward Gaza and the Mediterranean.
evidence.limits: Shabwa remained Hadhramaut's capital until late third century CE.

evidence.title: Taymāʾ & Dadan / Al-ʿUlā (NW Saudi Arabia): Walled caravan-oasis cities
evidence.dateBasis: Fourteen kilometers of Bronze-to-Iron stone ramparts around Taymāʾ, Nabonidus's 10-year Neo-Babylonian desert court (553–543 BCE) and Dadanite monumental cliff reliefs.
evidence.summary: Deep spring-fed palm oases walled off the Nafud Desert transformed Taymāʾ and Dadan into fortified Lihyanite and Minaean caravan crossroads long before Nabataean Hegra.
evidence.limits: Site layers span Bronze Age through Roman–Islamic centuries.

evidence.title: Tepe Sialk (Kashan) & Ecbatana / Hegmataneh (Hamadan, Iran): Ziggurat mound & Median capital
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1716 Hegmataneh mudbrick grid beside Tepe Sialk's 6th–1st millennium BCE Chalcolithic–Proto-Elamite–Iron Age mudbrick platform.
evidence.summary: Across the western Iranian plateau, Tepe Sialk documents early silver cupellation and Proto-Elamite tablets, while nearby Hegmataneh rose as capital of the Medes and summer seat of the Achaemenids.
evidence.limits: Hegmataneh continued directly into Parthian and Sasanian cities.

evidence.title: Gordion / Yassıhöyük (Sakarya Valley, Anatolia): UNESCO #1669 Phrygian citadel & pebble mosaics
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #1669 tree-ring, C14 and stratigraphic sequence anchored by the 8th-century BCE Early Phrygian Megaron Gate, geometric pebble floors and Tumulus MM ('Midas Mound').
evidence.summary: Commanding central Anatolia's Sangarius–Sakarya plain, Phrygian kings erected massive glacis stone walls, inlaid wooden furniture inside huge cedar tombs and geometric pebble palace floors.
evidence.limits: Abandoned as a fortified civic center after the 189 BCE Roman–Galatian campaign.

evidence.title: El-Omari & Maadi–Buto (Lower Egypt): Predynastic grain-silo villages & Levantine copper outpost
evidence.dateBasis: Calibrated radiocarbon dates linking subterranean Maadi stone-lined houses, copper ingots and donkey trade directly to Southern Levantine EB I caravans.
evidence.summary: Lower Egyptian villagers near modern Cairo lived in oval timber-and-mat huts surrounded by subterranean storage pits—and at Maadi built subterranean stone rooms echoing Beersheba architecture to smelt imported Palestinian copper.
evidence.limits: Gradually absorbed into expanding Upper Egyptian Naqada II–III cultural unification.

evidence.title: El-Badari & Naqada / Nubt (Upper Egypt): Predynastic agrarian towns & earliest social hierarchy
evidence.dateBasis: Sequence dating (Petrie seriation anchored by modern AMS radiocarbon) defining Badarian ripples-ware farming through Naqada I–II mudbrick towns and goldworking centers.
evidence.summary: On desert edges flanking the Upper Egyptian floodplain, Badari and Naqada ('Golden Town' near desert Wadi Hammamat gold reefs) pioneered fine ripple-burnished ware, ivory craft and elite regional chiefdoms.
evidence.limits: Predynastic towns sit largely beneath modern Nile cultivation or edge cemeteries.

evidence.title: Tell el-Farkha & Elephantine Island (Egypt): Delta Predynastic breweries to First Cataract fort
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified mudbrick brewery vats, golden foil statuettes and Lower/Upper Egyptian cultural transition at Tell el-Farkha, alongside Elephantine Nilometers & border town strata.
evidence.summary: In the eastern Delta, Tell el-Farkha brewed industrial beer and housed Early Dynastic ivories at the Asia caravan gate, while Elephantine controlled the rocky First Cataract portal into Nubia.
evidence.limits: Elephantine's urban strata extend through Greco-Roman and Late Antique eras.

evidence.title: Kadero & Kadruka (Central–Northern Sudan): Fifth-millennium pastoral Nile settlements & bucrania graves
evidence.dateBasis: Calibrated radiocarbon sequence from Khartoum Neolithic shell-mound villages, wild sorghum-imprinted pottery and cattle-horn prestige burials in Upper Nubia.
evidence.summary: Along elevated Nile paleochannel banks, Kadero and Dongola Reach Kadruka communities combined dense cattle pastoralism and sorghum harvesting with finely burnished ripple pottery and polished stone maceheads.
evidence.limits: Regional aridification shifted settlement closer to the active Nile channels after 3500 BCE.

evidence.title: Kawa (Gematon) & Musawwarat es-Sufra (Sudan): Kushite temple enclosures & desert hafir reservoirs
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated New Kingdom-to-Napatan–Meroitic mudbrick towns, Lion Temple inscriptions and colossal Great Enclosure sandstone corridors.
evidence.summary: At Kawa in the Dongola Reach and Musawwarat es-Sufra out in the Butana steppe, Kushite kings built monumental stone temples, elephant murals, workshops and massive rain-catchment hafir reservoirs.
evidence.limits: Meroitic pilgrimage activity at Musawwarat continued through the third century CE.

evidence.title: Sembel & Ona Villages (Asmara Plateau, Eritrea): First-millennium BCE stone agro-pastoral towns
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon dates from excavated dry-stone rectangular compounds, bull-head groundstone palettes and teff/barley granary pits across Greater Asmara.
evidence.summary: Long before Aksum rose, highland communities on the Eritrean plateau built densely packed stone towns herding humpless cattle and forging bronze-and-iron agriculture independently on the Red Sea rim.
evidence.limits: Survey coverage shows dozens of unexcavated Ona mounds around Asmara.

evidence.title: Akjoujt (Grotte aux Chauves-Souris, Mauritania): West Africa's earliest dated copper metallurgy
evidence.dateBasis: AMS & conventional radiocarbon dates on charcoal inside prehistoric copper-ore mining galleries and slag-tapped reduction furnaces (Lambert 1971; Vernet).
evidence.summary: Deep in western Mauritania's Guelb Moghrein hills, Chalcolithic miners followed malachite veins underground with grooved stone mauls and smelted over 160 documented copper axes, arrowheads and bracelets.
evidence.limits: Controversy persists on independent Saharan invention vs distant North African Mediterranean stimulus.

evidence.title: Dhar Oualata & Dhar Tagant (SE Mauritania): Stone-compound village confederacies
evidence.dateBasis: Extension of the Tichitt–Oualata tradition surveyed across hundreds of tiered dry-stone residential compounds with domesticated pearl millet temper.
evidence.summary: Built across sandstone escarpments overlooking seasonal Holocene lakes, dry-stone walled compounds linked sprawling pastoralist-millet chiefdoms that foreshadowed medieval trans-Saharan Sahel polities.
evidence.limits: Desiccation by ~400 BCE dispersed communities southward toward the Niger Bend.

evidence.title: Taruga & Samun Dukiya (Nok Heartland, Nigeria): Earliest dated West African iron & terracotta settlements
evidence.dateBasis: Bernard Fagg & Frankfurter Nok Project radiocarbon–TL dates tying dome-shaped iron-smelting furnaces directly to hollow terracotta sculpture and pearl-millet village pits.
evidence.summary: In wooded central Nigerian valleys south of the Jos Plateau, Taruga villagers fired dramatic life-size clay heads alongside thirteen bloomery iron-smelting furnaces as early as the first millennium BCE.
evidence.limits: Acidic forest-savanna soils dissolve unburned bone, limiting skeletal preservation.

evidence.title: Kursakata & Mege Mounds (Lake Chad Basin, Nigeria–Cameroon): Lagoon farming & iron emergence
evidence.dateBasis: Deep tell stratigraphy tracing post-Gajiganna clay-plain homesteads raising humpless cattle, pearl millet and Chad Basin fish as Lake Chad retreated.
evidence.summary: Along fertile firki clay plains left by shrinking Mega-Chad, rising settlement mounds like Kursakata and Mege shifted cleanly from bone-harpoon camps into settled Iron Age villages.
evidence.limits: Mounds remained inhabited well into the medieval Sao era.

evidence.title: Katuruka & Kemondo Bay (Buhaya, NW Tanzania): Urewe preheated-blast ironworking villages
evidence.dateBasis: Peter Schmidt's excavations pairing decorated clay tuyeres, charcoal-pit iron furnaces and classic Early Iron Age Urewe dimple-based pottery along Lake Victoria.
evidence.summary: West of Lake Victoria, Urewe communities constructed sophisticated conical bloomery furnaces preheating forced air via ceramic tuyeres to produce high-carbon steel for forest clearing and farming.
evidence.limits: Continuous Urewe–Buhaya ironworking continued into the 2nd millennium CE.

evidence.title: Hyrax Hill & Prolonged Drift (Central Rift, Kenya): Savanna Pastoral Neolithic stone settlements
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon dates from stone-circle house platforms, obsidian blades, Nderit/Elmenteitan pottery and dense cattle-sheep-goat herding middens overlooking Lake Nakuru.
evidence.summary: Above ancient Rift Valley lakes, Savanna Pastoral Neolithic herders laid out stone-enclosure homesteads herding cattle and small stock over two millennia before Bantu Iron Age arrival.
evidence.limits: Sirikwa Iron Age stone hollows later reused parts of the Hyrax Hill ridge.

evidence.title: Elands Bay Cave & Dunefield Midden (West Coast, South Africa): Terminal Pleistocene-to-100 BCE coastal base
evidence.dateBasis: John Parkington's tight shell-midden C14 sequence charting marine adaptation through sea-level rise, Wilton microliths and final pre-pastoral handprints.
evidence.summary: Opening above Verlorevlei lagoon on the Atlantic coast, Elands Bay Cave preserves tens of thousands of shellfish, crayfish and seal feasts crowned with dozens of Later Stone Age red-ochre handprints.
evidence.limits: A mid-Holocene hiatus reflects local aridity before dense late Holocene shell-mound surges.

evidence.title: Divuyu & Nqoma Forebears / Toteng Horizon (Northern Botswana): Earliest southern pastoral camps
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon-dated sheep/caprine bones, Bambata-ware pottery and early Okavango-margin camps charting livestock movement across the Kalahari corridor.
evidence.summary: Long before Iron Age stone towns, mobile Khoe-ancestral and Bambata-using communities tended sheep and goats along seasonal Botletli and Okavango waterways across northern Botswana.
evidence.limits: Small open campsites leave sparse architectural footprints compared with later stone kraals.

evidence.title: Utica & Kerkouane (Tunisia): UNESCO #332 Punic port & un-rebuilt Phoenician-Amazigh town
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO WHC #332 excavations at Kerkouane preserving untouched Punic courtyard houses, mosaic bathtubs and Tanit symbols abandoned intact during the Third Punic War.
evidence.summary: Unlike Carthage under Roman rebuilding, Cap Bon's seaside town of Kerkouane—and North Africa's oldest Phoenician colony Utica—preserve pure Punic-Libyan civic planning, dye vats and sanctuary courtyards prior to 146 BCE.
evidence.limits: Kerkouane remained abandoned after 146 BCE; Utica continued under Roman provincial rule.

evidence.title: Lixus & Mogador (Atlantic Morocco): Purple-dye & garum islands beyond Gibraltar before 100 BCE
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified Phoenician red-slip pottery at Mogador island (Essaouira) and monumental Mauretanian–Punic temple acropolis terraces at Lixus above the Loukkos River.
evidence.summary: Mariners from Tyre and Cádiz turned Atlantic Morocco into the westernmost industrial workshop of the ancient world—harvesting murex purple dye at Mogador and building the acropolis city of Lixus.
evidence.limits: Both sites experienced heavy Mauretanian–Roman expansion after 100 BCE.
